projectDesc.p: The digital part of the SNSF project 'Caroline Spurgeon: Chaucer Allusions, Shakespeare's Imagery, and the Digital Humanities' aims to create the first open-access database dedicated to the criticism and reception of Chaucer throughout history. It draws on the compilation and cataloguing work carried out by Professor Caroline Spurgeon (1869–1942) and collected in 'Five Hundred Years of Chaucer Criticism and Allusion'. This work consists of three volumes and a supplement, which will be systematically transcribed, corrected, enriched, encoded and published online, in order to facilitate future research and bring new perspectives to light.

editorialDecl.p: The original spelling and punctuation are retained. Meaningful layouts are reproduced, i.e. verses, printed marginalia, dots lines, tables, etc. However, we do not consider, the line breaks for prose, the columns or the curly brackets. The same rules apply for special characters and glyphs. Otiose letters are normalised, as well as spaces before punctuation marks.

ab.seg: [Vol. I contains: General Introduction; Life of Chaucer; List of his Works; Errata and Addenda; Introduction to the Romaunt of the Rose; Introduction to the Minor Poems. Text of The Romaunt. Text of the Minor Poems (23 pieces). Notes to the Romaunt and Minor Poems. pp. i-Ixiii, 1-568. (See also vol. iv below, for additions to Minor Poems). Vol. II contains: Introduction to Boethius; Introduction to Troilus. Text of Boethius. Text of Troilus. Notes to Boethius and Troilus. pp. i-lxxviii, 1-506. Vol. III contains: Introduction to House of Fame; Introduction to Legend; Introduction to Astrolabe: Plates illustrating the description of the Astrolabe. Texts of these Pieces. Critical Notes to the Astrolabe. Notes to the House of Fame, Legend and Astrolabe. An Account of the Sources of the Canterbury Tales. pp. i-lxxx, 6 plates, 1-504. Vol. IV contains: Introduction on the MSS. of the Canterbury Tales and their types, plan of the present edition, and a table of the ways of numbering the lines. The Introduction contains also Additions to 'The Minor Poems' in vol. i. These are XXIV. Womanly Noblesse. XXV. Complaint to my Mortal Foe. XXVI. Complaint to my Lode-sterre. 'Notes to the Preceding Poems' follow. Text of the Canterbury Tales, groups A to I. Appendix to group A. The Tale of Gamelyn. pp. i-xxxii, 1-667. Vol. V contains: Notes to the Canterbury Tales, with an Introduction on the Chaucer Canon; the editions of Thynne, Stowe, Tyrwhitt, Chalmers, Moxon; Later Works; Some of the Minor Poems; the Text of the Canterbury Tales; the Harley and Ellesmere MSS.; Dryden’s remarks on Chaucer's verse; scansion, accentuation; pronunciation; sources of the notes; acknow¬ ledgments. Notes on the tales (including Gamelyn) follow. Addenda. Index to the subjects, etc. explained in the notes. pp. i-xxviii, 1-515. Vol. VI contains: General Introduction, discussing the texts of the various pieces; obligations to others; æsthetic criticism; the dialect of Chaucer; Chaucer's Kenticisms; pronunciation, vowels, diphthongs, consonants, phonetically rendered; scansion and accents; open and close o and e, etc.; rime; assonances; final y and ye; stanzaic schemes; Chaucer as metrist; analysis of his language and grammar; versification. Glossarial Index. Glossary to fragments B and C of the Romaunt. Glossary to Gamelyn. Index of proper names. Index of authors quoted or referred to by Chaucer. Index of Books referred to in the Notes. List of MSS. General list of Errata. General Index, pp. i-ciii, 1-414. Vol. VII (Supplementary Volume), Chaucerian and other Pieces, contains: Introduction on the apocryphal pieces, generally and individually, and the texts as follows: I. Testament of Love (Usk). II. Plowman’s Tale. III. Jack Upland. IV. Gower's Praise of Peace. V. Horcleve’s Letter of Cupid. VI. To the Kinge's most noble Grace Horcleve. To the Lordes and Knightes of the Garter VII. Geogan's Moral Ballade. VIII. Lydgate’s Complaint of the Black Knight. IX. Lydgate’s Flour of Curtesye. X. Lydgate's Balade in Commendation of our Lady. XI. To my Soverain Lady (Lydgate). XII. Ballad of Good Counsel (Lydgate).¹ XIII. Beware of Doubleness (Lydgate). XIV. Balade Warning Men to Beware of Deceitful Women (Lydgate).¹ XV. Three Sayings (Lydgate). XVI. Ros's La Belle Dame sans Mercy. XVII. Henryson's Testament of Cressid. XVIII. Clanvowe’s Cuckoo and Nightingale. XIX. Envoy to Alison. XX. Flower and Leaf. XXI. Assembly of Ladies. XXII. Goodly Balade (Lydgate).¹ XXIII. Go Forth, King (Lydgate ¹ On the question of Lydgate's authorship of these pieces, see The Chaucer Canon, by H. N. MacCrachen, E. E. T. S., 1911, pp. xlviii-xlix XXIV: Court of Love. XXV. A Virelai. XXVI. Prosperity (John Walton). XXVII. Leaulte vault Richesse. XXVIII. Sayings printed by Caxton. XXIX. Balade in Praise of Chaucer. Notes. Glossarial Index. Index of Names. Index to some Subjects explained in the Notes. List of Subscribers. pp. i-lxxxiv, 1-628.] [vol. vi. In the first place, my endeavour has been to produce a p. ix] thoroughly sound text, founded solely on the best MSS. and the earliest prints, which shall satisfy at once the requirements of the student of language and the reader who delights in poetry. In the interest of both, it is highly desirable that Chaucer's genuine works should be kept apart from those which were recklessly associated with them in the early editions, and even in modern editions have been but imper¬ fectly suppressed. It was also desirable, or rather absolutely necessary, that the recent advances in our knowledge of middle- English grammar and phonetics should be rightly utilized, and that no verbal form should be allowed to appear which would have been unacceptable to a good scribe of the fourteenth century. I have also provided a large body of illustrative notes, many of them gathered from the works of my predecessors, but enlarged by illustrations due to my own reading during a long course of years, and by many others due to the labours of the [p. x] most recent critics. The number of allusions that have been traced to their origin during the past fifteen years is consider¬ able; and much additional light has thus been thrown upon Chaucer's method of treating his originals. ... The glossary has been compiled on a much larger scale than any hitherto attempted, wherein the part of speech of almost every word is duly marked, and every verbal form is sufficiently parsed. ... [p. xviii] As regards the texts, my chief debt is to the Chaucer Society, which means, practically, Dr. Furnivall, through whose zeal and energy so many splendid and accurate prints of the MSS. have been produced, thus rendering the actual read- ings and spellings of the scribes accessible to students in all countries. It is obvious that, but for such work, no edition of Chaucer could have been attempted without an enormous increase of labour and a prodigal expenditure of time.
